patient_information: A 7-year-old girl from a tropical region of a West African country. There is no history of relevant trauma or other systemic symptoms.
chief_complaint: Progressive skin ulcers on the right hand and wrist with associated hand contracture over a period of three months.
history_of_present_illness: The illness began three months prior after an insect bite, starting as an itchy papule on the back of her right hand that gradually enlarged. Initial treatments from a traditional healer with herbal remedies were ineffective. The lesion ulcerated a few weeks later, and she received diclofenac and dexamethasone at a local health post. A second lesion then appeared, and a course of oxacillin was initiated with no effect. Concurrently, she became progressively unable to use her right hand.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from a district in the tropical region of a West African country. The history mentions an insect bite, but this is considered an incidental finding as the mode of transmission for the causative organism is unknown.
vitals: Pulse was 108 bpm, blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, and temperature was 37.9°C (100.2°F).
physical_exam: The patient was an anxious girl in good general condition, holding her right wrist in a 45° flexion and 20° abduction position. Two skin ulcers were present: a 3 x 3 cm ulcer on the back of her right hand filled with necrotic tissue, and a 0.5 x 1 cm ulcer on the medial side of her right wrist. The ulcers were surrounded by an ill-defined induration (12 x 8 cm) with hypo- and hyperpigmentation, lichenification, desquamation, and oedema extending from the lower arm to the fingers. A 0.5 x 0.5 cm nodule was also noted above the medial right elbow.
labs_and_diagnostics: Laboratory confirmation was achieved via PCR from a wound swab, which confirmed the presence of Mycobacterium ulcerans.
differential_diagnosis: The primary suspected diagnosis was Buruli ulcer, based on the geographical region, patient's age, and clinical picture of progressive cutaneous ulcers on an extremity without major trauma. Other differential diagnoses for ulcers in tropical countries include various infectious (bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic) and non-infectious (trauma, envenoming, autoimmune, haematological, neoplastic) causes.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent 8 weeks of specific antimycobacterial therapy and wound care. During this period, the ulcer on the back of her hand healed almost completely, but the second, smaller ulcer paradoxically increased in size to 8 x 10 cm. Due to this, she required surgical debridement and skin grafting. The contracture of her wrist was corrected with physiotherapy, and she made an uneventful recovery.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was Buruli ulcer disease caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans. The diagnosis was strongly suspected based on the clinical presentation of progressive, necrotizing skin ulcers with surrounding induration and oedema, leading to a joint contracture in a child from an endemic region in West Africa. The diagnosis was definitively confirmed by a positive PCR test for M. ulcerans from a wound swab.
